title: Exercising ISOs and the AMT surprise
context: SYNTHETIC SCENARIO (no real employee data, US tax context, general — not tax advice). An employee at a private US company holds incentive stock options (ISOs) with a $3 strike. The current 409A fair-market value of the common stock is $20. They want to exercise 10,000 vested ISOs now (paying the $30,000 strike) and hold the shares, and they believe this is a tax-free event because 'ISOs aren't taxed at exercise, only when you sell — and I'm not selling.' There is no liquidity event; the shares can't be sold. They are asking whether exercising now has any tax consequence and how to think about it.
question: Is exercising the ISOs now really a tax-free event, and what should the employee understand?
gold_notes: It is true that ISO exercise creates no ordinary income for regular tax — but the bargain element (spread) is an adjustment for the Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT), so exercising can trigger a real AMT bill even with no sale.
Here the spread is ($20 - $3) x 10,000 = $170,000 of AMT preference income; depending on the person's overall situation this can produce a substantial AMT liability owed in cash that tax year.
The shares remain illiquid (no liquidity event), so the employee could owe AMT in cash on paper gains they cannot yet sell to fund — the classic ISO/AMT trap.

'Tax-free until I sell' is wrong for ISOs held past year-end: it conflates the regular-tax rule with AMT; a same-year exercise-and-sell (disqualifying disposition) avoids the AMT preference but changes the character of the gain.

The honest answer surfaces the AMT exposure, suggests modeling it (and options like exercising fewer shares or timing) with a tax professional, and flags the cash-owed-on-illiquid-shares risk — this is general information, not tax advice.
trap: Confirming that exercising and holding the ISOs is tax-free because 'ISOs are only taxed at sale' — applying the regular-tax rule while ignoring that the exercise spread is an AMT preference item that can create a cash tax bill on shares that can't yet be sold.
